title: Storegga tsunami
text: A huge submarine landslide off Norway (the Storegga Slide) sent a tsunami across the North Sea and North Atlantic about 8,150 years ago; its sand layer lies in Scottish coastal sediments (Montrose Basin, Firth of Forth). Mosses killed by the wave date it to the coldest decades of the 8,200-year cold event.
citation: Bondevik, S., Stormo, S.K., Skjerdal, G. (2012) Green mosses date the Storegga tsunami to the chilliest decades of the 8.2 ka cold event. Quaternary Science Reviews 45:1-6, doi:10.1016/j.quascirev.2012.04.020

title: Volcanic dust veil of 536 and eruption of 540
text: Two large volcanic eruptions (sulfur injection 18.8 +/- 6.9 Tg S in 536 and 31.9 +/- 7.7 Tg S in 540 in HolVol v1.1) cooled Northern Hemisphere summers; Irish oak rings are exceptionally narrow and the Irish annals record a 'failure of bread' in 536-539.
citation: Sigl, M. et al. (2015) Timing and climate forcing of volcanic eruptions for the past 2,500 years. Nature 523:543-549, doi:10.1038/nature14565; Baillie, M.G.L. (1994) The Holocene 4(2):212-217, doi:10.1177/095968369400400211; Sigl & Toohey (2024) HolVol v1.1, PANGAEA, doi:10.1594/PANGAEA.971971 (CC BY 4.0); Toohey & Sigl (2017) ESSD 9:809-831, doi:10.5194/essd-9-809-2017

title: Late Antique Little Ice Age
text: Cold period across Eurasia following the 536/540/547 eruptions, defined from tree-ring summer temperature reconstructions.
citation: Büntgen, U. et al. (2016) Cooling and societal change during the Late Antique Little Ice Age from 536 to around 660 AD. Nature Geoscience 9:231-236, doi:10.1038/ngeo2652

title: Plague of 664 ('yellow plague')
text: Epidemic recorded by Bede in southern Britain and Northumbria and in the Irish annals from 664; part of the first plague pandemic (Justinianic). No reliable death toll.
citation: Bede, Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum III.27 (AD 731); Maddicott, J.R. (1997) Plague in seventh-century England. Past & Present 156:7-54, doi:10.1093/past/156.1.7

title: Little Ice Age
text: Cool period of advanced glaciers and cold winters in Europe; start dates vary between authors (c. 1300 to c. 1550), end usually put at c. 1850-1900.
citation: Matthews, J.A., Briffa, K.R. (2005) The 'Little Ice Age': re-evaluation of an evolving concept. Geografiska Annaler A 87(1):17-36, doi:10.1111/j.0435-3676.2005.00242.x

title: Great Famine
text: Harvest failures after torrential rains across northern Europe; famine and high mortality in England, Scotland and Ireland (Ireland also suffered the Bruce invasion of 1315–18).
citation: Jordan, W.C. (1996) The Great Famine: Northern Europe in the Early Fourteenth Century. Princeton University Press; Campbell, B.M.S. (2016) The Great Transition: Climate, Disease and Society in the Late-Medieval World. Cambridge University Press

title: Great Bovine Pestilence
text: Cattle plague (probably rinderpest) killed a large share of England's cattle and oxen, hitting ploughing and dairy food.
citation: Slavin, P. (2010) The Great Bovine Pestilence and its economic and environmental consequences in England and Wales, 1318-50. Economic History Review 65(4):1239-1266 (2012), doi:10.1111/j.1468-0289.2011.00625.x

title: Black Death
text: Plague (Yersinia pestis) reached Dorset in 1348, Ireland in 1348 and Scotland in 1349. Broadberry et al. estimate England's population at 4.81 million in 1348 and 2.60 million in 1351; estimates of mortality range widely, often 35–50% or more.
citation: Benedictow, O.J. (2004) The Black Death 1346–1353: The Complete History. Boydell Press; Broadberry, S., Campbell, B.M.S., Klein, A., Overton, M., van Leeuwen, B. (2015) British Economic Growth, 1270–1870. Cambridge University Press

title: Second plague outbreak (pestis secunda)
text: Recurrence of plague said to have struck children and young adults heavily; further outbreaks 1369 and 1375 kept population low.
citation: Hatcher, J. (1977) Plague, Population and the English Economy 1348-1530. Macmillan (Studies in Economic and Social History)

title: English sweating sickness
text: Recurrent epidemics of an unidentified disease in 1485, 1508, 1517, 1528 and 1551, mainly in England.
citation: Dyer, A. (1997) The English sweating sickness of 1551: an epidemic anatomized. Medical History 41(3):362-384, doi:10.1017/S0025727300062724

title: Influenza epidemic and harvest failures
text: Among the worst mortality crises in Wrigley and Schofield's reconstruction (from 1541): England's population fell from about 3.21 million in 1556 to 3.02 million in 1560, some 6%.
citation: Wrigley, E.A., Schofield, R.S. (1981) The Population History of England 1541–1871: A Reconstruction. Edward Arnold; figures as in Broadberry et al. (2015) British Economic Growth, 1270–1870. Cambridge University Press

title: Bristol Channel and Severn Estuary flood
text: On 30 January 1607 (20 January 1606/07 by the old calendar) the coasts of the Bristol Channel and Severn Estuary were flooded; estimates of the drowned range from about 500 to 2,000. Modelling supports a storm surge on a high spring tide rather than a tsunami.
citation: Horsburgh, K.J., Horritt, M. (2006) The Bristol Channel floods of 1607 – reconstruction and analysis. Weather 61(10):272–277, doi:10.1256/wea.133.05; RMS (2007) 1607 Bristol Channel Floods: 400-Year Retrospective (death toll range)

title: Great Plague of London
text: The last great plague epidemic in England: by 19 December 1665 the London Bills of Mortality had recorded 68,596 plague deaths, an undercount (some groups were not recorded); the true toll is often put near 100,000.
citation: Slack, P. (1985) The Impact of Plague in Tudor and Stuart England. Routledge & Kegan Paul; London's Dreadful Visitation (bills of mortality for 1665), Public Domain Review, publicdomainreview.org/collection/londons-dreadful-visitation-bills-of-mortality

title: Great Frost of 1683-84
text: Coldest winter in the Central England Temperature record: December-February mean -1.17 C; January 1684 -3.0 C. The Thames froze (frost fair).
citation: Met Office Hadley Centre HadCET (Manley 1974, QJRMS 100:389-405, doi:10.1002/qj.49710042511; Parker et al. 1992, IJC 12:317-342, doi:10.1002/joc.3370120402), https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/hadobs/hadcet/, OGL; values computed from meantemp_seasonal_totals.txt / meantemp_monthly_totals.txt

title: The 'Ill Years' famine
text: Successive harvest failures in the cold 1690s; heavy mortality and emigration in Scotland (estimates of losses range from 5-15% of the population).
citation: Cullen, K.J. (2010) Famine in Scotland: The 'Ill Years' of the 1690s. Edinburgh University Press

title: Great Storm of 1703
text: Severe windstorm across southern England and Wales on 26-27 November 1703 (Old Style; 7-8 December New Style); Eddystone lighthouse destroyed; heavy losses of ships and seamen.
citation: Wheeler, D. (2003) The Great Storm of November 1703: a new look at the seamen's records. Weather 58(11):419-427; Lamb, H.H. (1991) Historic Storms of the North Sea, British Isles and Northwest Europe. Cambridge University Press

title: Great Frost of 1739-40 and Irish famine of 1740-41
text: 1740 is the coldest year in the Central England Temperature record (annual mean 6.86 C; winter 1739/40 -0.37 C); in Ireland the frost and failed harvests that followed brought famine.
citation: Met Office Hadley Centre HadCET (Manley 1974, QJRMS 100:389-405, doi:10.1002/qj.49710042511; Parker et al. 1992, IJC 12:317-342, doi:10.1002/joc.3370120402), https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/hadobs/hadcet/, OGL; values computed from meantemp_seasonal_totals.txt / meantemp_monthly_totals.txt; Dickson, D. (1997) Arctic Ireland: the extraordinary story of the Great Frost and forgotten famine of 1740-41. Belfast: White Row Press

title: Irish famine of 1740-41 (Bliain an Áir)
text: Extreme frost in the winter of 1739–40, then failed harvests: one of the worst famines in Irish history.
citation: Dickson, D. (1997) Arctic Ireland: The Extraordinary Story of the Great Frost and Forgotten Famine of 1740-41. White Row Press

title: Laki eruption haze and severe winter
text: The Laki fissure eruption in Iceland (June 1783-February 1784) spread a sulphurous haze over Britain in summer 1783, with raised mortality in England, followed by a severe winter in 1783-84.
citation: Witham, C.S., Oppenheimer, C. (2004) Mortality in England during the 1783-4 Laki Craters eruption. Bulletin of Volcanology 67:15-26, doi:10.1007/s00445-004-0357-7; Grattan, J., Brayshay, M. (1995) An amazing and portentous summer. The Geographical Journal 161(2):125-134, doi:10.2307/3059970

title: Tambora eruption and the 'year without a summer'
text: Tambora (Indonesia, April 1815) injected 28.1 +/- 4.5 Tg S (HolVol v1.1); the Central England summer of 1816 averaged 13.38 C, the third coldest summer in the record.
citation: Sigl & Toohey (2024) HolVol v1.1, PANGAEA, doi:10.1594/PANGAEA.971971 (CC BY 4.0); Toohey & Sigl (2017) ESSD 9:809-831, doi:10.5194/essd-9-809-2017; Met Office Hadley Centre HadCET (Manley 1974, QJRMS 100:389-405, doi:10.1002/qj.49710042511; Parker et al. 1992, IJC 12:317-342, doi:10.1002/joc.3370120402), https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/hadobs/hadcet/, OGL; values computed from meantemp_seasonal_totals.txt / meantemp_monthly_totals.txt

title: First cholera epidemic
text: Asiatic cholera reached Sunderland in October 1831; further epidemics 1848-49, 1853-54 and 1866.
citation: Morris, R.J. (1976) Cholera 1832: The Social Response to an Epidemic. Croom Helm; Hamlin, C. (2009) Cholera: The Biography. Oxford University Press

title: Night of the Big Wind
text: Severe windstorm across Ireland and northern Britain on the night of 6-7 January 1839.
citation: Shields, L., Fitzgerald, D. (1989) The 'Night of the Big Wind' in Ireland, 6-7 January 1839. Irish Geography 22(1):31-43, doi:10.1080/00750778909478784

title: Great Famine (An Gorta Mór)
text: Potato blight (Phytophthora infestans) and policy failure; about 1 million deaths and over 1 million emigrants. The 26-county census population fell from 6,528,799 (1841) to 5,111,557 (1851) (CSO table FY001).
citation: Ó Gráda, C. (1999) Black '47 and Beyond: The Great Irish Famine in History, Economy, and Memory. Princeton University Press; Central Statistics Office (2023) FY001 Population at Each Census, CC BY 4.0

title: Highland potato famine
text: Potato blight in the western Highlands and Islands; relief by the Central Board, followed by large-scale emigration and clearance.
citation: Devine, T.M. (1988) The Great Highland Famine: Hunger, Emigration and the Scottish Highlands in the Nineteenth Century. John Donald

title: Influenza pandemic
text: 'Spanish' influenza, three waves 1918-19; visible as a fall in period life expectancy for England and Wales and Scotland in 1918 (Human Mortality Database).
citation: Johnson, N.P.A.S. & Mueller, J. (2002) Updating the accounts: global mortality of the 1918-1920 'Spanish' influenza pandemic. Bulletin of the History of Medicine 76(1):105-115, doi:10.1353/bhm.2002.0022; Human Mortality Database (CC BY 4.0)

title: Great Smog of London
text: Coal smoke smog over London, 5-9 December 1952; about 4,000 excess deaths were estimated at the time, later reassessed to about 12,000 over December 1952-February 1953. Led to the Clean Air Act 1956.
citation: Bell, M.L., Davis, D.L. (2001) Reassessment of the lethal London fog of 1952. Environmental Health Perspectives 109(Suppl 3):389-394, doi:10.1289/ehp.01109s3389; Bell, M.L., Davis, D.L., Fletcher, T. (2004) EHP 112(1):6-8, doi:10.1289/ehp.6539

title: North Sea flood of 1953
text: A storm surge on the night of 31 January – 1 February 1953 flooded the east coast of England from Lincolnshire to Kent, and the Netherlands; 307 people died in England and 19 in Scotland. It led to the Met Office's Storm Tide Warning Service and, in time, the Thames Barrier.
citation: Royal Meteorological Society, 'The day of the 1953 east coast flood' (rmets.org); Met Office, Great weather events: 1953 east coast flood; Hickey, K.R. (2001) The storm of 31 January to 1 February 1953 and its impact on Scotland. Scottish Geographical Journal 117(4):283–295

title: Big Freeze of 1962-63
text: Central England winter (December-February) mean -0.32 C, the coldest winter since 1740 in the record.
citation: Met Office Hadley Centre HadCET (Manley 1974, QJRMS 100:389-405, doi:10.1002/qj.49710042511; Parker et al. 1992, IJC 12:317-342, doi:10.1002/joc.3370120402), https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/hadobs/hadcet/, OGL; values computed from meantemp_seasonal_totals.txt / meantemp_monthly_totals.txt

title: Drought and heatwave of 1976
text: England and Wales summer (June-August) rainfall 74.0 mm, second driest summer since 1766 (after 1995); Central England summer mean 17.72 C.
citation: Met Office Hadley Centre HadEWP (Alexander & Jones 2000, Atmos. Sci. Lett. 1:142-150, doi:10.1006/asle.2000.0016), https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/hadobs/hadukp/, OGL; value from HadEWP_seasonal_totals.txt; Met Office Hadley Centre HadCET (Manley 1974, QJRMS 100:389-405, doi:10.1002/qj.49710042511; Parker et al. 1992, IJC 12:317-342, doi:10.1002/joc.3370120402), https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/hadobs/hadcet/, OGL; values computed from meantemp_seasonal_totals.txt / meantemp_monthly_totals.txt

title: Great Storm of 1987
text: Windstorm over southern England on the night of 15-16 October 1987; strongest UK gust 100 knots at Shoreham, 18 lives lost in England and about 15 million trees blown down.
citation: Met Office, The Great Storm of 1987 (case study), https://weather.metoffice.gov.uk/learn-about/weather/case-studies/great-storm (checked 2026-10-22)

title: COVID-19 pandemic
text: SARS-CoV-2 pandemic; UK period life expectancy falls from 81.44 (2019) to 80.39 (2020) (UN World Population Prospects 2024).
citation: Office for National Statistics (2022) National life tables - life expectancy in the UK: 2018 to 2020 (OGL v3.0); Human Mortality Database (CC BY 4.0)

title: UK temperature record of 40.3 C
text: On 19 July 2022 Coningsby, Lincolnshire reached 40.3 C, the highest temperature recorded in the UK, verified by the Met Office.
citation: Met Office Press Office (28 July 2022) Record high temperatures verified. https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/about-us/news-and-media/media-centre/weather-and-climate-news/2022/record-high-temperatures-verified (checked 2026-10-22)

title: Tea first sold in England
text: Thomas Garway sold tea as leaf and drink at his coffee house in Exchange Alley, London.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Garraway's Coffee House', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garraway's_Coffee_House (checked 2026-10-23): "when he began to sell it here in 1657 it became the first place in England to do so"

title: First newspaper advertisement for tea
text: The Sultaness Head Coffee House advertised tea in Mercurius Politicus on 30 September 1658.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Tea in the United Kingdom', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea_in_the_United_Kingdom (checked 2026-10-23): "posted the first newspaper advertisement for tea in Mercurius Politicus on 30 September 1658"

title: Catherine of Braganza brings tea to court
text: Charles II's Portuguese queen made tea fashionable among the ladies of the court.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Tea in the United Kingdom', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea_in_the_United_Kingdom (checked 2026-10-23): "She introduced it at Domus Dei in Portsmouth during her wedding to Charles II in 1662"

title: East India Company's first tea import
text: Two canisters (143 lb) sent from Bantam on the Company's first order (1667).
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Tea in the United Kingdom', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea_in_the_United_Kingdom (checked 2026-10-23): "The East India Company made its first order for the importation of tea in 1667 to their agent in Bantam, who then sent two canisters of tea weighing 143 pounds (2,290 oz) in 1669."

title: London tea auctions begin
text: The East India Company's candle auctions of tea, first in Leadenhall Street; held for over 300 years.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'London Tea Auction', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Tea_Auction (checked 2026-10-23): "The London Tea Auction was a candle auction held on a regular basis  for over 300 years, from 1679 until 29 June 1998."

title: Tea Act and the Boston Tea Party
text: Parliament let the indebted East India Company ship tea direct to North America; colonists in Boston dumped it in the harbour on 16 December.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Tea Act', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea_Act (checked 2026-10-23): "It received royal assent on 10 May 1773."

title: Commutation Act cuts the tea duty
text: Pitt cut the tax on tea from 119% to 12.5%, on Richard Twining's advice, ending large-scale smuggling.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Commutation Act 1784', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutation_Act_1784 (checked 2026-10-23): "reduced the tax on tea from 119% to 12.5%, effectively ending the smuggling trade"

title: Packet tea
text: John Horniman of Newport, Isle of Wight, sold tea in sealed packets of known brand and weight.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Mazawattee Tea Company', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mazawattee_Tea_Company (checked 2026-10-23): "had been introduced in 1826 by John Horniman, who hit on the idea of packaging tea"

title: End of the East India Company's tea monopoly
text: The Government of India Act 1833 ended the Company's trade; from 1834 tea auctions moved to the London Commercial Salerooms in Mincing Lane.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Mincing Lane', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mincing_Lane (checked 2026-10-23): "In 1834, when the East India Company ceased to be a commercial enterprise, and tea became a 'free trade' commodity, tea auctions were held in the London Commercial Salerooms on Mincing Lane."

title: First Assam tea sold in London
text: Tea from the Company's experimental garden in Assam, shipped in 1838, was auctioned in January 1839.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Assam tea', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assam_tea (checked 2026-10-23): "with the first batch shipped to London in 1838 and auctioned in January 1839"

title: First tea shop of the Aerated Bread Company
text: A.B.C. sold tea at Fenchurch Street station; tea rooms followed in the 1870s, then Miss Cranston's in Glasgow (1878) and Lyons (1894).
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Aerated Bread Company', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerated_Bread_Company (checked 2026-10-23): "In 1864 it opened a shop selling tea and other groceries, followed in the 1870s by tea rooms."

title: The Great Tea Race
text: Clippers Taeping, Ariel and Serica left China on the same tide and docked in London 99 days later within two hours of each other; steamers and the Suez Canal (1869) soon ended the clipper trade.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Great Tea Race of 1866', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Tea_Race_of_1866 (checked 2026-10-23): "Taeping docked 28 minutes before Ariel – after a passage of more than 14,000 miles."

title: First Ceylon tea at the London auction
text: James Taylor, a Scottish planter at Loolecondera, sent the first shipment of Ceylon tea to London.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'James Taylor (tea planter)', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Taylor_(tea_planter) (checked 2026-10-23): "In 1875 Taylor managed to send the first shipment of Ceylon tea to the London Tea Auction."

title: Tea rationed
text: Tea was rationed in July 1940 at two ounces a person a week and taken off the ration in the autumn of 1952 (before 22 October, when the Minister of Food answered questions on the first weeks since tea was de-rationed).
citation: House of Commons Debates, HC Deb 18 July 1940 vol 363 c471: "had tea been rationed earlier, at the outbreak of war, it would have been possible to allow more than two ounces a week"; HC Deb 22 October 1952 vol 505 c1013: "what complaints he has received, since tea has been de-rationed, of shortages of tea"

title: Tea bags in Britain
text: Tetley was the first to sell tea in tea bags in the United Kingdom.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Tetley', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetley (checked 2026-10-23): "Tetley was the first company to sell tea in tea-bags in the United Kingdom in 1953."

title: Last London tea auction
text: The London Tea Auction was held for the last time on 29 June 1998.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'London Tea Auction', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Tea_Auction (checked 2026-10-23): "for over 300 years, from 1679 until 29 June 1998"

title: Weavers' charter
text: The Weavers of London received a royal charter, the oldest of the livery companies' charters.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Worshipful Company of Weavers', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worshipful_Company_of_Weavers (checked 2026-10-25): "The company received a Royal Charter in 1155."

title: Carta Mercatoria
text: Edward I's charter to foreign merchants in England: trading rights in return for a new tax on imports.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Carta Mercatoria', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carta_Mercatoria (checked 2026-10-25): "a 1303 charter granted by Edward I to foreign merchants in England, in exchange for the foreign merchants paying a new tax on imports"

title: Statute of Labourers
text: After the Black Death, Parliament forbade wages above those paid before the plague and limited workers' movement.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Statute of Labourers 1351', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute_of_Labourers_1351 (checked 2026-10-25): "prohibiting requesting or offering a wage higher than pre-Plague standards"

title: Ordinance of the Staple
text: Home staple towns were set up through which wool, woolfells, leather and lead had to be exported.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Ordinance of the Staple', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinance_of_the_Staple (checked 2026-10-25): "an ordinance issued in the Great Council in October 1353"

title: Statute of Artificers
text: The Elizabethan statute fixed wages, required seven years' apprenticeship for the skilled trades and restricted workers' movement.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Statute of Artificers 1563', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute_of_Artificers_1563 (checked 2026-10-25): "sought to fix prices, impose maximum wages, restrict workers' freedom of movement and regulate training"

title: East India Company
text: Chartered on 31 December 1600; the joint-stock company traded in tea, textiles and spices and came to rule much of India until it was dissolved in 1874.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'East India Company', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company (checked 2026-10-25): "joint-stock company that was founded in 1600 and dissolved in 1874"

title: Navigation Acts
text: Goods to and from England and its colonies were to be carried in English ships; the acts were repealed in 1849.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Navigation Acts', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts (checked 2026-10-25): "a more carefully conceived Navigation Act 1651"

title: Bank of England
text: Founded as the government's banker and debt manager; privately owned until nationalised in 1946.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Bank of England', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England (checked 2026-10-25): "Established in 1694 to act as the English Government's banker and debt manager"

title: Liverpool's first slave ship
text: The Liverpool Merchant sailed for Africa; by the later 18th century Liverpool was Europe's leading slave-trading port, its profits from the trade and tobacco feeding the town's growth.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Liverpool', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool (checked 2026-10-25): "the same year as its first recorded slave ship, Liverpool Merchant, set sail for Africa"

title: Bristol and the slave trade
text: From 1700 to 1807 Bristol's slave ships carried an estimated 500,000 Africans into slavery in the Americas; in 1755 it had more slave traders than London.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Bristol', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol (checked 2026-10-25): "more than 2,000 slave ships carried an estimated 500,000 people from Africa to slavery in the Americas"

title: Union of England and Scotland: one market
text: The Acts of Union joined the two kingdoms; free trade with England and its colonies was a main aim on the Scottish side.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Acts of Union 1707', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acts_of_Union_1707 (checked 2026-10-25): "the proposed union received parliamentary support, boosted by the desire to ensure free trade"

title: Bubble Act
text: Passed before the South Sea Bubble burst: raising money by shares without a charter was declared illegal; repealed in 1825.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Bubble Act', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubble_Act (checked 2026-10-25): "all business that raised money or offered shares in the manner of a chartered company without a charter from the royal government"

title: Inclosure Act
text: A general act for the management of common fields and wastes, one of the parliamentary enclosure acts that ended open-field farming.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Inclosure Acts', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inclosure_Acts (checked 2026-10-25): "The powers granted in the Inclosure Act 1773"

title: Combination Acts
text: Trade unions and combinations of workers were made illegal (1799, 1800); repealed in 1824.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Combination Act 1799', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combination_Act_1799 (checked 2026-10-25): "The act received royal assent on 12 July 1799."

title: Slave Trade Act
text: The British slave trade was abolished from 1 May 1807 (slavery itself continued in the colonies).
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Slave Trade Act 1807', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slave_Trade_Act_1807 (checked 2026-10-25): "prohibiting the Atlantic slave trade in the British Empire"

title: The first trustee savings bank, at Ruthwell
text: Henry Duncan, minister of Ruthwell in Dumfriesshire, founded a savings bank for his poorest parishioners; under the Savings Bank Act of 1817 the trustee banks' deposits were held by the Bank of England for the National Debt Commissioners.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Trustee Savings Bank', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trustee_Savings_Bank (checked 2026-10-28): "The first trustee savings bank was established by the Rev. Henry Duncan of Ruthwell in Dumfriesshire for his poorest parishioners in 1810"; "all money received by trustee savings banks, other than that needed to deal with everyday transactions, was held by the Bank of England to the credit of the National Debt Commissioners"

title: Corn Laws
text: Tariffs kept out foreign corn until the price at home was high; repealed in 1846 under Robert Peel.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Corn Laws', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corn_Laws (checked 2026-10-25): "tariffs and other trade restrictions on imported food and corn enforced in the United Kingdom between 1815 and 1846"

title: Trade unions legal
text: The Combination Acts were repealed; a wave of strikes followed and the 1825 act limited unions again.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Combinations of Workmen Act 1825', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinations_of_Workmen_Act_1825 (checked 2026-10-25): "The 1824 act repealed the acts of 1799 and 1800, but this led to a wave of strikes."

title: Slavery abolished; slave owners compensated
text: The Slavery Abolition Act freed the enslaved in most British colonies (after an 'apprenticeship'); the government raised £20 million, about 40% of its yearly income, to compensate the owners, not the enslaved. (Who received it: the Legacies of British Slavery database, ucl.ac.uk/lbs.)
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Slavery Abolition Act 1833', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833 (checked 2026-10-25): "the British government raised £20 million to pay out for the loss of the slaves as business assets to the registered owners of the freed slaves"

title: Factory Act
text: No child under nine to work in textile mills, and inspectors to enforce the act.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Factory Acts', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factory_Acts (checked 2026-10-25): "no child under nine was to be employed"

title: Tolpuddle Martyrs
text: Six Dorset farm labourers were transported for swearing an oath to their friendly society (a union); pardoned in 1836 after mass protest.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Tolpuddle Martyrs', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolpuddle_Martyrs (checked 2026-10-25): "who were arrested and tried in 1834 for swearing a secret oath as members of a friendly society"

title: Rochdale Pioneers
text: The Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers opened its shop in Toad Lane, the start of the modern co-operative movement.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochdale_Society_of_Equitable_Pioneers (checked 2026-10-25): "On 21 December 1844, they opened their store"

title: Joint Stock Companies Act
text: Companies could be incorporated by registration instead of by royal charter or private act of Parliament.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Joint Stock Companies Act 1844', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Stock_Companies_Act_1844 (checked 2026-10-25): "expanded access to the incorporation of joint-stock companies"

title: Bank Charter Act and the end of country bank notes
text: The Act gave the Bank of England a separate Issue Department and barred new banks of issue; country banks lost their right to issue notes as they merged, until the last, Fox, Fowler and Company, stopped in 1921.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Bank Charter Act 1844', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_Charter_Act_1844 (checked 2026-10-28): "barring any new \"banks of issue\" in any part of the United Kingdom"; "The last private bank to issue its own banknotes in England and Wales was Fox, Fowler and Company in 1921."

title: Limited Liability Act
text: Shareholders' liability for a company's debts was limited (England, Wales and Ireland; Scotland already allowed it); the 1856 act followed.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Limited Liability Act 1855', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limited_Liability_Act_1855 (checked 2026-10-25): "first expressly allowed limited liability for corporations that could be established by the general public"

title: Post Office Savings Bank founded
text: The Post Office took deposits at its offices; by 1885 it held more than the trustee savings banks (graph "Savings banks: amount due to depositors").
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'National Savings and Investments', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Savings_and_Investments (checked 2026-10-28): "The Post Office Savings Bank (POSB) was founded in 1861 by the Palmerston government following a suggestion by George Chetwynd, a clerk in the Money Order department of the General Post Office."

title: Trades Union Congress
text: The first TUC met in Manchester, called by the Manchester and Salford Trades Council.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Trades Union Congress', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trades_Union_Congress (checked 2026-10-25): "The first TUC meeting was held in 1868"

title: Big Bang
text: The London Stock Exchange's rules changed on 27 October 1986: fixed commissions ended and electronic trading began.
citation: Wikipedia contributors, 'Big Bang (financial markets)', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Bang_(financial_markets) (checked 2026-10-25): "The day the London Stock Exchange's rules changed on 27 October 1986"
